messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Marcus

Marcus was fifty-two years old when a student's father came to his office after school on a Tuesday in March. The man had been drinking. He was angry about a disciplinary decision Marcus had made that morning—a suspension for his son, who had been caught dealing pills to classmates. The conversation escalated quickly. Marcus remembered trying to de-escalate, to explain the school's policy, but the man had shoved him against the filing cabinet, and then there was a moment of pure chaos: the man's fist coming at his face, Marcus's arm up to block it, the sharp pain in his ribs as the man drove his shoulder into him, the smell of whiskey and rage, the feeling of being utterly trapped in his own office with the door closed. It lasted perhaps ninety seconds. A secretary heard the noise and called security. The man was arrested. Marcus went to the hospital, was treated for bruising and a hairline fracture of the fourth rib, and was sent home.

That was fourteen months ago. In the intervening year, Marcus had returned to work, had pressed no charges, had tried to move forward. But something had fractured inside him that extended far beyond bone.

The memories had begun almost immediately—not as narrative recollections he could summon at will, but as intrusive replays that arrived without warning. He would be sitting at his desk reviewing budget reports when the film would start: the man's face looming toward him, the sound of knuckles hitting the cabinet an inch from his head, the sensation of his own ribs compressing under impact. The memories came with such vividness and immediacy that his body would respond as though the attack were happening again. His chest would tighten. His arm would move into a protective position. His breath would come short. When he tried later to deliberately reconstruct what had happened—to talk to his wife Sarah about it, to give a coherent account to his therapist—the details scattered. He could access fragments: the man's red face, the word "suspension," the cold metal of the cabinet. But the whole sequence, the precise order of events, the exact words spoken, remained stubbornly inaccessible, as though his mind had filmed the event but then encoded it in a language he could no longer read.

And the threat monitoring had become relentless. Marcus had always been observant—a good principal notices everything—but now his awareness had narrowed into a constant scanning apparatus. The moment he entered any room, his eyes moved to the exits. In the school hallway, he found himself cataloguing potential weapons: the heavy bookend on a shelf, the letter opener on a colleague's desk, the way a student might grip a water bottle. In restaurants, he positioned himself with his back to the wall. At home, he noted where the kitchen knives were kept, whether the front door was locked, the weight of the baseball bat in the garage. This hypervigilance had begun as a rational response—a way of ensuring he would never be trapped again—but over months it had become involuntary, a background hum of threat assessment that colored every environment.

The memories themselves had become the trigger that launched this threat response. When the film played—and it played unpredictably, several times a day—Marcus's body would flood with the conviction that danger was present. His startle response had become exaggerated; he would jump at a colleague's knock on the door, his heart racing as though the man were there again. The vividness of the memory, the way his body reenacted its defensive posture, created a present-tense sense of peril that his rational mind could not override. He would look around the room, searching for the threat that his nervous system had just told him was imminent, and find only ordinary school furniture and afternoon light. But the searching continued anyway, compulsive and exhausting.

Sarah had noticed the changes first. Marcus had always been a steady presence—organized, measured, the kind of man who helped other families through crises. But he had become withdrawn, irritable when she asked him about his day. He no longer went to the gym. He had stopped attending the monthly principals' association dinners. Six months after the assault, he had asked to move their bedroom to the ground floor, closer to the exits. When Sarah questioned this, he could not articulate why, only that it felt necessary. The distance between them had widened in the way that unspoken fear creates distance—she could feel that something was wrong, but Marcus could not find words for the constant vigilance, the way his own mind had become an unsafe place.

What had finally brought him to seek help was a moment last week when he realized he could not remember his daughter's college graduation ceremony. He had been there, had taken photographs, had stood at the edge of the crowd. But the memory was gone—not forgotten, but inaccessible, as though it had happened to someone else. In its place was a vague awareness that he had spent the afternoon scanning the auditorium for exits and watching the hands of people in the crowd. He had missed his own daughter's moment, and the loss of that memory, that presence, had broken something in him. Marcus had called a therapist and made an appointment. What he most wanted was to reclaim his life from the man who had spent ninety seconds in his office. What he feared most was that the man had already won.
